speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: MR. WINKLER  PRODUCTION OF DOCUMENT REFERRED TO BY POSTMASTER GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege which concerns all hon. members of this house and, of course, the whole country. Yesterday a motion for the production of papers was on the order paper, motion No. 99, and there was an extended discussion with regard to the existence of a certain document. In the course of that discussion it was stated by the Postmaster General that this document did not exist. These words are to be found in Hansard at page 3626. A little earlier the Secretary of State also stated that the document did not exist. This was in accord with discussions which took place during consultation between the Secretary of State and the Post Office Department.
For the benefit of the house and the country, I have such a document before me now. As a matter of fact it is a copy of the document in question the production of which was requested under the terms of motion No. 99. If the house so desires I am prepared to table it, and that would end the discussion.

subtopic: MR. WINKLER  PRODUCTION OF DOCUMENT REFERRED TO BY POSTMASTER GENERAL
speechtext: Agreed.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
subtopic: MR. WINKLER  PRODUCTION OF DOCUMENT REFERRED TO BY POSTMASTER GENERAL
speechtext: I am advised that this is not a public document. It belongs to a private member; and if a private member is to produce a document of this nature-I have not seen the document but I assume it is of the nature indicated-the consent of the private member concerned would be required.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: MR. WINKLER  PRODUCTION OF DOCUMENT REFERRED TO BY POSTMASTER GENERAL

If may say a further word, the main point at this juncture is not whether the list which I have is authentic, though I believe it to be so. It is that the Secretary of State misled the house yesterday when he said this particular document did not exist. Also, if the words of the Secretary of State were clear, and I believe they were, then of course the Postmaster General had misled the Secretary of State as he misled the entire house.
As I have already indicated, I believe this document to be authentic. It is as set out in the notice of motion for the production of papers, and I would therefore ask leave of the house, by unanimous consent, since that
has been requested of me, to table this document.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Secretary of Stale) moved:
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext:
That commencing on Thursday, October 17, 1963, and on every Thursday and Friday thereafter until

the end of the current session, the hours of sitting on these days shall be:
Thursdays:
2.30 p.m. to 6 p.m., and from 7 p.m. to 10.30 p.m. Fridays:
11 a.m. to 1 p.m., 2.30 p.m. to 6 p.m., and from 7 p.m. to 10.30 p.m. and, in relation thereto, the provisions of standing order 6 shall be suspended; and
That on Wednesday, October 23, 1963, and on every Wednesday thereafter until the end of the current session, the hours from 5 to 6 p.m. in such sittings shall be used for government business and, in relation thereto, the provisions of standing order 15(3) concerning private members' business shall be suspended.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I had hoped that either yesterday or today it might have been possible, by agreement, to have the suggestions made in the motion now before the house accepted. I have been advised that, although the suggestions put forward in this motion are based upon the usual consultations that are held in these matters, and although I was advised that these suggestions would be acceptable to all parts of the house except the official opposition, they are not acceptable to the official opposition.
The advice I received was that the official opposition-I would be glad to be corrected at once if I am misrepresenting the situation in any way, because I have no desire to do that-would prefer a different arrangement which would involve the house meeting at 2 p.m. instead of 2.30 p.m. every sitting day and reassembling at 7 p.m. on Mondays, Tuesdays and Thursdays, and there would be no sitting on Friday evening.
I am very hopeful that this matter can be settled in as non-controversial a way as possible. Since there has been no reference to Wednesday, and since the suggestion with regard to Wednesday, if I remember correctly, came originally from the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, I assume the suggestions with regard to Wednesday are agreeable to all parts of the house.
I feel I owe the house and the opposition an explanation of the reason the government does not feel this alternative proposal would be acceptable. It is the feeling of the government that any attempt to meet at 2 instead of 2.30 would occasion delays in getting on with the business of the house which some of us feel, sir, are too great even when we meet at 2.30. It would mean that these hours of additional time would be given to something other than the purpose of the government in making these suggestions at all, that is in gaining additional time for dealing with government business.
Of course to meet at seven o'clock on Mondays and Tuesdays for the next four weeks would be totally useless for that purpose. The only result would be that an extra hour on

each of those days, that is to say eight extra hours, would be taken up with these supply motions. While the government has no desire in any way to abbreviate the time now provided for them, it would not at all serve the only purpose the government had in mind in making any suggestion of extending the hours, which was primarily to give additional time for the consideration of the estimates. Under the rules these hours for that purpose would be totally useless.
Therefore the effect of the suggestion made by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre would be to gain a few minutes in the early part of each day-how many it is hard to say-and one other hour, whereas our suggestion as put forward in the motion would provide six additional hours of useful time for the consideration of the public business.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext: What about Tuesdays, is not that public business?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext:
No. As the hon. member, who at one time was presiding officer of this house and for whose opinions we have the greatest respect, must realize, it is the right of the representatives of the people to expose their grievances before they agree to do the public business. The government has no desire to abbreviate that time for the exposure of grievances, but that time is not devoted to the public business. Certainly it is devoted to public affairs, but not to the public business in the sense of the business a government has to put before the house.
Last Friday the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre indicated, when I made the suggestion and which I am grateful to the house for accepting, that he was acutely conscious of the problem that is faced by the government and the house in dealing with the estimates. As a matter of fact I thought he expressed the problem very much better than I did in his exposure of it, and I have no quarrel with anything he said at that time.
I think I also ought to point out to hon. members and to you, sir, that if the house is disposed to accept the motion that I am now proposing it would be the intention of the government, unless some unforeseen or exceptional circumstances should arise, to take the time on Thursday and Friday evenings from now until the end of the session for estimates; and it would be the intention, until we had dealt with the principal departments of government, to take a new department on each day so there would be an opportunity to have every department exposed to hon. members, in order that they could express their views about the policies of the government and bring up any points with respect to it.
Extension of Hours of Sitting
It would also be the intention of the government to fix the days on which departments would be take nsufficiently far in advance so that hon. members would know what was coming and would therefore be in a position to deal in an orderly way, without surprise, with these various departments.
Until November 12 what I have suggested would mean, if it is accepted by the house, that on Mondays and Tuesdays we would spend our time on supply motions, and up until that time we would take every Thursday and Friday evening for the consideration of estimates. All that would leave to the government for the consideration of its legislative program-which hon. members who look at the order paper can see is quite extensive- would be the brief time on Wednesdays and a somewhat longer time than usual on Thursdays, although there would not be much difference because of the extra hour on Wednesdays, and of course a little longer time on Fridays, because on Friday we sit in the morning. Hon. members would know those three days would be devoted normally to legislation, and the two evenings would be devoted to the estimates.
The only alternative that the government thinks is feasible, if the house is to do the business we were elected to do and sent here to do, is to have Saturday sittings. The government would rather not have them- much rather-and I think the house would rather not have them. It did seem to us- and I think this was the view of all those who discussed this matter through the usual channels-that if we could have available these extra five hours of sitting, which is after all not a great deal of additional time- and I have several interesting observations by the Leader of the Opposition when he was on this side of the house, on that particular point-and they were made available in the way I suggest, it would not put any undue burden on any hon. member. It would, moreover, have this great advantage; that we would not have to resort to morning sittings, which are very difficult for hon. members who are trying conscientiously to serve on committees, and are very difficult also for the government because, as hon. gentlemen on the front benches opposite will know the government does require some time to give consideration to the matters it is going to bring before the house if the business of the house is to be carried on in an orderly way.
It is because we do not believe we could conscientiously go on and hope to dispatch the business required to be dispatched before the end of this session, and end it in this calendar

Extension of Hours of Sitting year, that I am reluctantly putting this motion forward without the unanimous consent which I had hoped, and indeed rather expected, would be forthcoming when the discussions took place among the representatives of the other groups. I think it will be no secret in any part of the house that in fact I did make some modification in the proposal I was then making, in order to meet the suggestions put forward and in an attempt to accommodate the opposition. I simply state that as a fact.
I had hoped that by proceeding in the most conciliatory manner possible we could have a real understanding about this question and not take up a lot of the time of the house in discussing how and when we would do the business that it is our duty to do.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it would be rather unfortunate if the time of the house were taken up in a lengthy debate on a problem such as this, but this is the type of thing that perhaps happens when pressure is put on a house unnecessarily. Despite the problems that face this parliament, we nevertheless must recognize the fact that on both sides of this house we now have more people who have had experience of government than was the case for 22 years. This parliament, in so far as the Liberal party and the Conservative party are concerned, is in a better position to settle problems such as the sitting hours of the house because on both sides we know the responsibilities of an opposition and the responsibilities that weigh upon a government. So there is no better time than this year, by consultation and agreement, to settle the method of conducting the affairs of this parliament.
I think it is rather unfortunate that the house leader has presented us with the motion for debate today without further consultation, and without amendment to that motion. In discharging our responsibilities as an opposition we recognize the fact, and have often stated, that we think the hours of sitting of the House of Commons should be extended. I have been of that opinion for many years. There we have agreement; we are in favour of extending the hours.
Then we come down to deciding how the hours should be extended. In this particular instance we have an alternative suggestion to make which I relayed to the house leader's office yesterday noon. I understand the objections to morning sittings. We found out from our experience on the government side that morning sittings are not the best by any means. Every hon. member realizes that with House of Commons committee work going on, morning sittings are awkward, so we agree


with the house leader that morning sittings might be ruled out at the present time.
The house leader suggested that our proposal for meeting at two o'clock in the afternoon rather than 2.30 would not materially add to the conduct of the business of this house. With that I disagree. Meeting at two o'clock rather than 2.30 would add half an hour per day to our sittings, and that half hour would be used just as effectively as the half hour from 2.30 to 3, or, as it used to be in days gone by, from 3 to 3.30. So I do not see the value of his argument with regard to ruling out two o'clock as the time for assembly of this house.
The house leader bases a great deal of his argument on the fact that we still have before us four supply motions. He says that it is the government's intention to take these four supply motions during the next four weeks. This strikes me as quite unnecessary. There are nine weeks still available between now and the last week before Christmas, and supply motions are normally spread out and not crowded together one after the other. May I point out to the house leader that on some occasions in this house not all of the supply motions have been used. It has occurred on more than one occasion as the session has drawn to its close that the opposition has not made use of a supply motion That is a consideration which might be before us in this particular parliament. I think it would be very unwise indeed to crowd in four supply motions in the next four weeks, rather than to get on with government legislation and spread out the supply motions over the next nine weeks. Four in a row would be, in my opinion, extremely bad.
The house leader is concerned at the passing of the estimates for this year. I pointed out the other day that in an election year, the calendar year in which an election occurs, the house should very properly telescope the time for consideration of estimates. That was done in the election year of 1953 and also in the election year of 1949. It was not done in the election year of 1957 or the election year of 1962. But that is where the opposition plays its part, and I was making the very co-operative suggestion that this year, an election year, the time spent on estimates might very well be shortened; and it lies within the hands of the opposition to do that very thing.
I had hoped that the house leader would have come half way with me on that. An opposition realizes its position when it makes an offer of that sort, and in the interests of the proper conduct of business I think this should be considered by oppositions which

have a responsibility to this parliament just the same as the people on the government side. Then again the official opposition party, in its turn, should be considering that it will form the government of the future, and parliament then continues by a proper method. So there is a responsibility on an official opposition which is not enjoyed perhaps by other groups on the opposition side of the house.
I am not entering into the controversy with regard to how estimates were dealt with in the calendar year 1957 and the calendar year 1962, which makes a full story in itself. But I am suggesting that for this year, an election year, as responsible people we might make some arrangement which will fit into the problem facing the house leader, and at the same time discharge our duty to the country. I think estimates should not be brushed to one side, as some people infer from the suggestion put before us, because there are people here who will argue that the primary duty of parliament when it assembles is to deal with supply, to conduct the business of the country; that the secondary duty-or if you do not want to put it as secondary it is certainly on the same level-is to concern itself with legislative matters. But there are many legislative items on the order paper which are simply amendments to acts now on the statute books, and it would be difficult to argue that some of those items are of the same pressing urgency as the passing of supply for the conduct of the business of this country. So estimates should not be just brushed to one side; they should be brought forward and dealt with, and dealt with quickly. There are people here who will argue effectively that the estimates for each year should be brought forward much more rapidly than they have been during the last ten years.
Now, Mr. Speaker, unless the house leader is prepared to let his motion stand and continue further consultations among the parties of this house, I will be obliged to move an amendment to this motion. I wait for a response from the house leader. If he is willing to let this stand and consult again with the various parties I will not move an amendment, and this debate might be terminated within 30 seconds.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. gentleman would not mind indicating the kind of amendment he has in mind. I could not be expected to reach a conclusion without knowing what I was talking about.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext:
I am prepared to indicate that our suggestion will add not just five hours to the sitting hours, but five and a half. It will increase the weekly sittings from 25 J hours to 31, and it means adding
Extension of Hours of Sitting half an hour each day at the opening of the house-that is to say, coming in here at two o'clock instead of 2.30 Monday through Friday -and shortening the dinner hour and coming back into the house at seven o'clock on Monday, Tuesday and Thursday. There are three hours there, so you have an addition of five and a half hours to the time that we engage in this house.
Then may I also point out that those of us who have been here a number of years know perfectly well that when we approach the end of a session the house generally agrees without formal motion to sit the extra hours which are required in the last two weeks, whether it is Wednesday night or Friday night or a Saturday. I am opposed to Saturday sittings as early as this in a session. We tried that out one year and it was a failure. But I am not opposed, and I do not think the members of the Conservative party are opposed, to sitting say on two Saturdays some time in December if that is necessary to pass some of the unfinished business. But all this can be arranged as the business of the house progresses. If it is not agreeable to the house leader to consult on this matter, I would therefore move that-

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman should have an answer to his question before he puts the motion, and I am afraid the answer must be the answer I have already given; namely, that the government does not regard the half hour each day as being effectively half an hour, particularly as on Mondays and Tuesdays we would not be dealing with government business. The hour on Mondays and Tuesdays for the next four weeks, so long as we have supply motions, will not facilitate what we have in mind. Therefore I think the hon. gentleman should put his amendment.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext: Under the amendment which has been suggested a total of three and a half hours would be available to the government and a total of three hours would be of benefit to the opposition. In the light of the way this house is divided, surely the Secretary of State would agree that all the matters discussed in this house constitute public business. I would point out too that the opposition is, in a sense, under the gun, because there are to be four supply motions in a row, a situation which is altogether unprecedented. The hon. gentleman may shake his head, but I repeat that it is unprecedented to arrange our business in this way. I would hope, therefore, that the Secretary of State would see fit to accept the suggestion made by my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING

I think the hon. gentleman might as well put his motion.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we in this group have already intimated our intention to co-operate in the adoption of hours of sitting outlined in the motion.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext: Naturally.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext:
Yes, naturally, because we have learned a few things even though members of the official opposition have not. We have indicated our readiness to co-operate because we are convinced that if this house is to discharge its responsibilities to the people of Canada there has to be some way of expediting the progress of business. We felt the suggestions which were made were such as to help us in the discharge of those responsibilities. We are prepared to carry through the commitment we made when the representatives of the parties met together.
A number of suggestions have since been made as to how the motion might be modified so as to make it more acceptable to everyone. Reference has been made to the four supply motions which it is proposed shall be discussed week by week. Opposition has been expressed to this arrangement because, it is stated, the motions are being crowded together when they ought to be spread out. However, I am sure every member who was here at the time realizes that last year they were spread out so far that we never did get to them. I am sure we do not want a repetition of what took place on the last occasion as far as the estimates are concerned.
The house leader of the official opposition party intimated that he and his colleagues had learned something while they were in office, that they did not believe morning sessions were beneficial. There are other things which perhaps they should have learned in that connection. But we are convinced that one of the important tasks before us is to get the business of the nation taken care of and the estimates passed, after due consideration, in order that we shall not find ourselves being asked to vote interim supply month by month

until practically the whole year's estimates have been dealt with in this way.
Therefore we are prepared to support any action which would help us to accomplish the business before us.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext:
think we as members of the House of Commons ought to be concerned about the public image which we are projecting on the Canadian scene. I believe that in the eyes of the Canadian public we are making a ludicrous spectacle of parliament. Everyone knows the heavy agenda which still faces the House of Commons. Most of the departmental estimates have still to be dealt with and, in addition, there are vital pieces of legislation on the order paper. There are debates which ought to take place on public policies and public programs. In spite of all this we have spent at least half of the time since we reassembled on September 30 in carrying on a partisan wrangle as to whether it is the Liberals or Conservatives who are most responsible for the mess we are in. I submit that the people of Canada do not care how we got into the mess. They want to know how we are going to get out of it.
We in this party conceive it to be the duty of the opposition to scrutinize spending, to deal with the estimates, to examine legislation critically, and to offer alternative policies, and to do all this as expeditiously as possible. We do not deem it to be the function of the opposition to carry ori a program of obstruction which would grind parliament to a halt so that the government is reduced to a state of impotence; for if the government is reduced to a state of impotence it reflects not only upon the government but upon parliament itself.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext: A good speech to have made last year.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext:
Members of the Conservative party refer to last year, and I am prepared to agree that there was a program of obstruction carried on last year. I submit that this is precisely what is bedeviling the present session of parliament; the official opposition has spent most of its time fighting last year's battles instead of dealing with the problems which confront us today.
We in the New Democratic party are suggesting three things which we think might be done to expedite the business of this house. The first is that we pass the motion which has been presented by the Secretary of State.
The amendment which has been offered by the member for Winnipeg South Centre suggests an increase of five and a half hours a week in our sittings, three hours of which

will be used up in debating supply motions. This will do nothing to provide additional time for the transaction of government business. All it will do will be to enable a longer period of debate on motions of no confidence. We do not think the amendment will meet the siutation which confronts the house. It might be that modifications could be arrived at by agreement. However, I understand the house leaders have met and have done their very best to resolve the matter, without success; and as in my view the government's proposal is not unreasonable I think the house should accept it.
The second proposal this party wishes to place before the house is that we should give some consideration, for this session only, to dispensing with two of the supply motions. There are four remaining, and if the Leader of the Opposition is correctly reported in the press he has said he intends to move no confidence amendments to all four of these supply motions. This means that two days out of every week for the next four weeks will be spent debating these no confidence motions. Forty per cent of the time will go in debating no confidence motions.
In a normal session of parliament I certainly would fight very hard for the retention of the maximum amount of time the opposition is allowed to move motions of no confidence and to censure the government where they think that is necessary, but with the tremendous program before the house now and all the things we have to do in the very limited period of time remaining we would be prepared to forgo two of these supply motion debates. If there is not general agreement on that, could we agree to limiting the debate on each supply motion to one day, having one or two speakers from each of the major parties and one from each of the smaller parties and confining the debate on these supply motions to one day each? This would give us another four days which could be devoted to public business.
I noticed that the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre objected to the idea of calling four supply motions one right after the other, yet at the same time he is crying for the estimates to be discussed. He cannot have it both ways, and I think the sooner the departments are opened up, the sooner we get a chance to express our opinions on these various departmental estimates and to ask the government questions, the better it will be.
The third suggestion I wish to make is one I indicated yesterday. I should like to see us agree to proceed with the motion now on the order paper to set up the parliamentary committee to review the procedures of the house,
Extension of Hours of Sitting and do so either without debate or with agreement among the parties to restrict the debate to one or two speakers from each party. I think it is imperative that this committee be set up with the least possible delay.
One reason we are in difficulty in this parliament, as we were in the last one, is the fact that we are operating under procedures which were established to meet the pace of the Victorian era and not to cope with the tremendous volume of business confronting us in this modern age. When I first entered the House of Commons government expenditures were a little over $500 million. Today they are twelve times that amount. There are a great many more departments and a great many more programs than there were then, and we are going to have to revise the procedures of the house if we are going to carry on public business with efficiency and dispatch.
Therefore we suggest these three things; that we accept the motion, pass it and get down to business; that the house leaders or, if necessary, the party leaders consider cutting down the remaining supply motions to two for this session only, or restricting the debate to one day if that can be arranged; and that we set up the parliamentary committee to review the procedures of the house, either without debate or with a very limited period of debate.
I am convinced that if we do these three things we can carry on the public business of Canada with efficiency and dispatch. What is equally important, we can convey to the people of Canada the impression, which they do not now have, that we are serious about making parliamentary government effective and efficient.

Extension of Hours of Sitting Wednesday because that is the day for consideration of private bills. It seems to me that if we expect to get a lot of work done, the best time to do that work is when we are fresh after a rest on the week end. Logically Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday would be the best time. No other day has as many working hours as are now proposed for Friday. I should like to see these suggestions discussed, bearing in mind the fact that the most important point is already agreed upon, namely that we would all like to sit longer hours. Why can we not work out a sensible agreement? I do not think this one is sensible.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on behalf of the New Democratic party to register our opposition to the motion for concurrence in the second report of the standing committee on privileges and elections.
There are three things which I wish to make very clear at the outset of my remarks. First, I wish to make it clear that at the conclusion of my remarks I shall move an amendment. My amendment will be in the form that is provided in connection with committee reports. The gist of it will be that the house should instruct the committee to reconsider the matter and make another recommendation proposing that the members of groups on this side of the house, other than those in the official opposition, be seated in the house according to the numerical strength of the groups to which they belong. I shall develop that proposal later, but I just wish to make it clear that that is the position we in this party take.
The second point I wish to make clear, although I am sure it must already be very obvious, is that we in the New Democratic party have nothing whatever to gain by our opposition to the motion for concurrence. We have nothing whatever to gain by the terms of the amendment I shall move. The committee's report recommends that our party be moved up in this house to a position alongside the official opposition. I say, therefore, we have nothing to gain. As a matter of fact, if as a result of our debating this motion it were, in the end, to be defeated, we would have something to lose. It must be clear, therefore, that we are taking the stand we do on the basis of principle.
The third thing I wish to say, Mr. Speaker, is that our stand has nothing to do with whether we like or dislike any member or any group of members in this house. This does not matter one iota. I confess that having sat alongside the members of the Social Credit group, speaking of them in their totality, I have come to feel, if I may be so presumptuous as to say so, that a member like the hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Lessard) is the type of member we like to have in this house. He is making a good contribution. I do not stop there. I like the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Girouard). I like the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Ouellet).

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE

Privileges and Elections like the tactics of the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire). speechtext:
I gather that there is fairly general support for that proposition. However, the fact is that I was elected. I am here, and I have my rights. The 13 members who now say that they are supporters of the hon. member for Villeneuve were elected as members of the House of Commons. They were elected just as clearly as was the hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Pearson) or the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) or any of the other hon. members who are here. They have their rights. We must consider a matter such as that which is now before us, not on the basis of what we think about members or what we think about parties, but on the basis of what is the correct thing for us to do.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the question which has arisen results from the fact that a group of members who, when the house met in May, were united, has fallen into two sections or two units. As a result, before we came back on September 30, a request was made to Your Honour by each of these groups to be recognized and seated as a group. This matter, at Your Honour's suggestion, was referred to the standing committee on privileges and elections.
In my submission the only issue that faced us, the only issue that was really before the standing committee on privileges and elections, was the question of the seating arrangements in this House of Commons. I think the standing committee has gone completely off base by going into the area of making a decision as to what parties are to be recognized in this house, and what party or parties are not to be recognized. In totalitarian states the governments, the majorities, decide what parties are official and what parties are not official, but in no free democracy has any parliamentary majority or government the say as to what party is official and what party is to be recognized.

Privileges and Elections
The aspect which strikes me as offensive about the report, concurrence in which has been moved, is that it seems to imply that the New Democratic party is to be recognized as such, and that the Social Credit party is to be recognized as such. In the case of these two groups we wish that recognition; but then the report says that the other 13 hon. members, who say they wish to be known by a certain name and to be recognized as such, are not to be given the same treatment and consideration as is given to other groups in the house. They are referred to in the report not by any name they themselves have chosen but as a group of members under the leadership of the hon. member for Villeneuve, and although they are referred to as a collection in that way. they are treated as second class in that the report says that the question of their privileges should be studied by an officer of the House of Commons, who in turn should report to Your Honour.
I think there is a lot that is wrong with that fourth part of the report, and even if the house does not accept the amendment I propose I hope it will delete that fourth part. The two main things wrong with it are that it refers to an officer of the house a matter that, if it is to be decided at all, should be decided by Your Honour, and second that it makes a distinction between groups in the House of Commons. It says two of the smaller parties in the house have a right to certain recognition and a right to the names they chose, but the third smaller party in the house is in a second class position.
I stress the point that we do not like it when we hear of countries in other parts of the world where a government declares a certain party is not to be allowed or is not official. We have not liked it in the history of the past when in some countries certain parties have been eliminated from the state altogether. We are not doing that. No one is denying the right of these 13 members to be in the house. They cannot be denied that right under our free democratic system; but to take a step in that direction, when a majority of the committee or a majority of the house makes a decision, when it puts it on the record of the house that first one party is official and has its place, that another party is official and has its place in the house, but that a third group does not have the same rights and that its privileges must be referred to someone for study, I submit that in principle this is dangerous, and that it establishes a precedent that could come back to haunt us in the days that lie ahead.
In our Hansard every Wednesday we have a list appended thereto of the members of the House of Commons, and at the end of each

line is the party designation that a member chooses. The names are there, and it has never been submitted to a vote of the house as to whether members have the right to have their party designation as they wish it. Why, we even have one member of the cabinet, and we understand it is a Liberal government that is in power, whose party designation in every Wednesday's Hansard differs from that of all others on that side of the house. He is the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys. Has it ever been submitted to a decision of the house whether he can call himself Liberal-Labour rather than Liberal?
The fact is that across the years each party in the house has changed its name at one time or another. That goes for all of us.

speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yes; read the Parliamentary Guide. You will find there was a day when the Liberal party was known as the Laurier Liberals and at times they were the Liberal Progressives. The Conservatives were Liberal Conservatives, Progressive Conservatives and National Conservatives. We all have had our different names but, Mr. Speaker, no party has ever had to get approval by parliament of its name or its status.
We come here as individual members elected to represent our constituencies. I recall the debate which we had on a bill introduced by the former member for Wetaskiwin, Mr. Thomas, calling for the party names to be put on the ballots at election time, and the suggestion was that it be done merely for identification purposes. Some of us supported that bill but the overwhelming majority, the Liberals and the Conservatives, opposed it, using mainly the argument that men and women get elected not as candidates of a party but as members who on being elected represent the whole of a constituency, and that when they came to parliament they should be free to exercise their judgment as to where they sit and what they support. The question of what hon. members do is left to the individual hon. member.
I assert that it will be a sorry day if, by a majority vote of this house, we say certain parties are official and that one party is not official and is not to be recognized. The Liberal party has never been voted on by the House of Commons, either as to its name or as to its status as a party. This has never been done for the Conservative party either. The Conservative party never had to submit its constitution to parliament and never had to prove that its leader was properly elected. We never had to do that in the days of the C.C.F., nor have we had to do so as New Democrats.

We do not want a motion passed that parliament recognizes us. We do not need the recognition of a majority of the house. That could be given one day and taken away the next. We are a free party in a free country, in a country that emphasizes the principles of political democracy, and we will take a wrong step if we approve what is in the motion before the house at this time.
I stress the point that this has nothing to do with what advantage we gain from it. We have nothing to gain by opposing this motion. It has nothing to do with which members of which group in the Social Credit aggregation that we favour. We think the basic principle, of whether or not a majority decides that a party is official or not official, is a very serious matter.
I know that some will say there are various precedents from the past to look at it in this respect. I myself pointed out on September 30, when I first raised the point of privilege, that in 1935 and 1940 the C.C.F. groups in those parliaments were seated ahead of the Social Credit groups of those days, despite the fact that Social Credit had more members in each of those parliaments. I indicated on the basis of that precedent that I had contended in 1962 that it should be followed in our case at that time. That was refused. The house accepted the decision of Mr. Speaker Michener, confirmed by Mr. Speaker Lambert, that the numerical strength was the point that counted.
If I may review the previous instances, it is true that there are at least three instances when parties smaller in size sat higher than larger parties. There were the two cases I have just now referred to, when the C.C.F. party sat ahead of the Social Crediters. The other interesting case in history was in the 1921-25 parliament, when the Conservatives had fewer members than the Progressives and yet were the official opposition.
In all three of these cases, where smaller groups sat ahead of the larger groups, there was no contesting of the matter. In no case did the larger group contest the right of the smaller group. In the 1921 case the larger group did not want the position of official opposition, but in all cases where a larger group has asserted its right to be seated ahead of the smaller group it has been accepted, as happened in 1962 and 1963 when the Social Crediters were seated ahead of us. However, I repeat that in 1962 we established the principle that numerical strength is what counts.
I would say we were making a mistake if we were to change that principle and go back to the other one, back to the principle of history or what have you; but what this
Privileges and Elections report does is even worse. This report is based on both principles. It seats the New Democratic party first among three smaller parties because it has the larger number, because we have 17 members and the other groups have 13 and 11 respectively; but having started with that principle it changes in midstream and seats 11 members ahead of 13 members, on the argument that the 11 members presented themselves to the electorate as a party in the election of 1963, and on the contention that the others did not do so.
I ask hon. members, where in the elections act is there anything that says parties present themselves to the people as such? I ask hon. members, where in the Senate and House of Commons Act, or the British North America Act, or in Beauchesne or standing orders is there anything to support the contention that there is some point on the basis upon which people are presented to the electorate at election times? We come here as individuals. We come here free to move about. In most parliaments an individual here or there changes from one party to another. There have been changes of government. For example, in the 1926 parliament a government was defeated and another party moved over and formed the government. There were changes during the first world war. Parliament is not confined to the situation that obtains on any day; it consists of individual members of parliament who have the right to use their best judgment as to whom they should support and whom they should oppose.
It seems to me, therefore, that on principle there is no question about what we should do; that is, stick with the question of numerical strength which was accepted in the last parliament and in this one, and which has always been accepted whenever a larger group contended that it should be seated above a smaller group. Mr. Speaker, there are some-

Mr. Speaker, some hon. members and some people have asked questions about this in the newspapers. They are wondering about the $4,000 that was provided for in the bill of last July for leaders of parties, other than the official opposition, having 12 or more recognized members in the house. This section of that act has been quoted by some people as defining a party. I do not think it does anything of the kind. It merely gives a definition with respect to
3666	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Privileges and Elections the person who shall receive this extra $4,000.
I think it is rather unfortunate that this should confuse the issue. But I would like to point out that any suggestion now being made that a person cannot receive that extra allowance unless he presented himself to the electorate at election time as the leader of a group going to come into the house raises the question of what happened in the parliament of 1940 to 1945. Dr. Manion was the leader of the Conservative party in that election. He lost his seat. When the party came into the house it chose Hon. R. B. Hanson to be its house leader. He was not chosen at a party convention; he had not presented himself to the electorate as the leader of the official opposition. He was chosen by his group in the house as their leader, and he drew the salary of the leader of the official opposition. In 1942 he resigned from that position and the Conservative group in the house-and some of them are still here- chose the late Gordon Graydon to be their house leader. Having been elected by the majority of his group in the house, the largest group on the opposition side, he drew his salary as leader of the official opposition.
I suggest that to argue now that because the hon. member for Villeneuve was not the leader of the party at election time he therefore cannot be so considered is really trying to twist the statute to make it read the way one wants it to read. Maybe there are legal arguments as to why he is not entitled to the $4,000, but surely that is a matter for the courts to decide. We have passed a statute. We do not interpret our own statutes; I do not think that is up to us at all. I think, if I may say so, that is one point I was able to make before the committee on privileges and elections. It was agreed there that we had nothing to decide about that matter. I only mention it because it has come into the argument. But I suggest the point that should be considered is the position that obtained in the 1940 to 1945 parliament.
As I have already said, although some may wonder why I am stressing the point, we have nothing to gain by pressing this amendment, because the report if adopted moves us up next to the official opposition and if my amendment carries, so far as we are concerned there will be the same result. Therefore we are not grinding our own axe; we have nothing to gain. Neither are we defending the principles of those who follow the hon. member for Villeneuve because of any sympathy for their policies. We do not believe in them; everybody knows that. I have already indicated any likes or dislikes I might personally have, but I think it is that sort of thing we have to put aside.

I address my appeal particularly to the members on the Liberal side of the house and I ask them to face up to the position they find themselves in because of this motion. Here is a division of opinion between the 11 members of the Social Credit party, whose recognized leader is the hon. member for Red Deer, and the 13 members of the Rallie-ment des Creditistes, whose leader is the hon. member for Villeneuve. Here is a division between them as to which group should be seated closer to the Speaker, the 11 or the 13. One group will vote for itself, the other group will vote for itself. It is how the Liberals vote that will determine the issue. It does not matter how the Conservatives and New Democratic party vote; we cannot affect the issue; we will be outnumbered by the Liberals and either Social Credit group. Whether we vote one way or the other, it is the Liberal vote that will determine the outcome of this issue.
This means that in this House of Commons -as was the case in the committee on privileges and elections-the Liberal party will be making the decision as to which of these two parties comes ahead of the other.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: If a decision is made that 11 take priority over 13, it will be the Liberals who make the decision; it will be the Liberals who will have to defend it; it will be the Liberals who will have to give the country the rationalization for that decision. It will take on the appearance of the Liberals having wanted it a certain way and therefore just finding the arguments or reasons to do it. So I urge very strongly, Mr. Speaker, that the house consider the seriousness of this question. It is not just this group of members, because they may all be out after the next election.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Some of us might even hope they are defeated at the next election, but this kind of treatment will not defeat them. This kind of treatment, if given to their representatives in this house, will make them heroes, will make them martyrs back where they come from and might cause them to come back here in larger numbers after the next election than they have now.
Apart from that, I contend that the crucial thing we are dealing with today is whether in our kind of parliamentary democracy, in our kind of free society, it lies with any government or any majority of the House of Commons to make a decision which says that certain parties are official and a certain group which wishes to be known as a party is not official.

We went into all the history and the story of the Granby convention in the committee on privileges and elections. We went back into the origins of the Ralliement des credi-tistes and the origins of the Social Credit party, but I think this is irrelevant. Here we have a simple situation. We have three smaller parties, 17, 13 and 11 in numbers, each of which is claiming a position according to its numerical strength; and any attempt to alter that numerical strength is, I suggest, pushing things around the way one wants them for some unexplained, undeclared reason.
As the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquit-lam said a short time ago on another matter, this would not be good for parliament as a whole. We need to be concerned about the image parliament is projecting to the country at this time. I do not think it would improve the image we are projecting if parliament by its majority decided that 11 was more than 13, and that the 13 are not to have the privileges accorded to the others. This would not be good for the reputation of parliament.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin):
That the second report of the committee on privileges and elections be not now concurred in but that it be referred back to the said committee with instruction to amend it so as to recommend that members of the opposition who belong to groups other than the official opposition be seated in the House of Commons according to the numerical strength of their respective groups.
Mr. Speaker, you will notice that that amendment says nothing at all about recognition of groups. We do not need to be recognized by a vote of the House of Commons, any more than do the Liberals or Conservatives. Neither does the Social Credit party nor the Ralliement des creditistes. The amendment deals with the only thing which, in my view, we have the right to deal with, which is a procedural arrangement-the arrangement of the seating of members of this House of Commons. I think this amendment avoids the pitfall which is in the main motion, and I earnestly hope the house will give serious consideration to it.
I know that in the standing committee on privileges and elections when I moved a similar amendment it was defeated overwhelmingly. The only people voting for it were the members of the New Democratic party and the representative of the Ralliement des creditistes; the others voted the other way. But in the meantime this matter has been discussed in the public press. There have been editorials on it, and I think even some members of the committee have had second thoughts. I hope we will avoid taking a step which just seems to be doing what

Released by Martin Kelin, national president of the Social Credit Association of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, before pursuing this line, I should like to call the attention of the house to the official constitution of the national Social Credit party. And I was saying a minute ago, this constitution can be changed only when a national convention is held. Now, as the hon. member for Lapointe alleged in his testimony that the Granby convention was a national convention, I wish to quote some articles from our constitution concerning notification of a national convention.
A national convention shall be held every four years or more often, as may be decided by the national council.
The convention shall meet at a time and a place determined by the national council, but a three months' notice, announcing the date and place, shall be given to affiliated organizations and to members in general where there is no provincial organization.
Mr. Speaker, this procedure was not followed, since nobody from the other provinces was invited to the said Granby convention, in order that the said convention might become a national convention, and even Social Credit members living in provinces other than Quebec were not invited.
Consequently, the national convention in Granby had no authority whatever to change the status of the national leader of the Social Credit party, which leader, as is so well prescribed in our regulations and constitution, must be chosen only at a national convention.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to quote other excerpts from the testimony of the member for Lapointe, and this to prove how much he could contradict himself in such a short time. At a certain moment, the hon. member for Lapointe said:
The group, Ealliement des creditistes, having chosen a new leader, it is a fraction of Social Credit which withdrew from the main group.
And this, after having said in his testimony that we had withdrawn and not they.
Whom should we believe, in the circumstance? How is it possible to believe the statements of the hon. member for Lapointe, who never stops contradicting himself each time he is confronted with the facts.
On the other hand, the hon. member for Lapointe duly recognizes Mr. Thompson as the leader of the Social Credit party. In order to justify his stand he stated:
Mr. Thompson came only once to the province of Quebec to speak about the deepening of the Matapedia river.
And as I said earlier, he did not come to my riding during the last election campaign, nor did he go to any other riding of the province of Quebec, except to start off the campaign, and all along our campaign we referred to Real Caouette as leader of the Ralliement des creditistes and deputy leader of the national party.

Most important, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that if the members belonging to the group of the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) think that they can, after an election where they were elected under one name, change that name, I think that would be misrepresentation before the electorate.
In fact, if we reduce the argument ad absurdum, we could say that, in 1958, if the party in power, the Conservative party, had decided to divide into two groups after the election, that is 140 members in power and 68 in the official opposition, we would have had an intolerable situation where the Conservative party would have acted at the same time as the party in power and as the official opposition.

Once
Privileges and Elections they have gone to the people squarely, I think there will not be any problem as to the recognition of the privileges to which they are entitled, the same as any hon. member of this house.

We submit, Mr. Speaker, that this is false representation to the electors. If the people had known before the election that those members were to follow such a course of action, they would probably not have been elected.
Mr. Speaker, nothing in the Social Credit program would have led one to expect a split in our ranks at a given moment, and that, following that split, we would have to recognize a group under the leadership of the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) and another under the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson). If the electors had known that, I am sure the vote would have been different.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I do not intend to follow the hon. gentleman in the arguments he has presented to the house concerning the internecine strife between a group of members who have divided themselves into two groups. This is a matter for them, and not for the House of Commons. I agree that the stand taken by the house on this matter should have been submitted to a committee for the fullest consideration. This committee met under the chairmanship of the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron). I have read the evidence taken and the discussions that took place in the committee. I feel that further evidence should have been taken, for when one reads the two volumes he can only conclude that the subject was dealt with more by failure to face the issues than by actually facing them.
I point out that, in so far as the recommendations that are made are concerned, there are several that I do not believe parliament can accept if it has any regard for the heritage of parliament and its traditions, as well as the respect which parliament must have if it is to function properly. In so far as recommendation No. 1 is concerned, that the New Democratic party occupy seats next to the official opposition on the left side of the

Privileges and Elections Speaker, I think there will be general agreement in that regard.
The next recommendation is that the members of the Social Credit party occupy the seats next to the New Democratic party on the left side of the Speaker. I find it difficult to understand how, in the face of the evidence, the committee could have arrived at that conclusion, for it denies every principle that we have accepted in parliament. In so far as the party led by the hon. member for Vil-leneuve (Mr. Caouette) is concerned, I strongly disagree with many of the views expressed by that leader. Frankness demands that I say that I disagree with them. However, this is a democracy and the words of Voltaire were never more applicable than they are here. He said, "I disapprove of what you say but will defend to the death your right to say it." I apply those words of Voltaire to the situation today, and say to the hon. member for Villeneuve that I accept the principle inherent in that declaration, provided that what is spoken is not treasonable, treacherous or in any way inimical to the state. In other words, I accept that principle so long as what is said is within the law.
No parliament can exist unless each member has the freedom, under the law, to say what he believes. We go farther than that. There is no one in the galleries of this House of Commons, either the public galleries or the press gallery; that is the tradition of parliament. It goes back to the days of Charles I when the battle was being fought for the freedom of parliament and of parliamentarians to say what they wished. Neither the Governor General nor his representatives can sit in the gallery. The reason is a simple one. If they were there, there may be exercised by them some control over the freedom of the members to speak as they wish.
I say again that I dislike some of the declarations that have been made by those in this house led by the hon. member for Villeneuve. However, we do not choose members of parliament on the basis of a common agreement to say the same thing in parliament. If we all speak alike, then democracy dies. On the other hand, when I think of some of the attacks made on the hon. member for Villeneuve, I feel that the house should be reminded there was a time when he enjoyed political respectability. He was a Liberal candidate in the general election of 1956, and made a very good run at that time. This, however, is background material.
Why has this controversy arisen? Well, the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) was chosen as the leader. As one follows him through the peregrinations of debate in this


house, one might almost conclude he was sitting on the other side of the house. Indeed, I was in his constituency the other day and there were widespread rumours of the possibility of a change in that regard not being too far distant. However, that is beside the point. These are things we have to consider.
What is a political party? In summarizing the situation when you brought this matter before parliament, Mr. Speaker, you referred to the definition made by that tribune of democracy, Edmund Burke. None of us can understand parliament unless we know history. There is no more interesting reading, interesting to Canada because of its significance to this nation, than the debate in the British parliament beginning on February 25, 1791 on the Quebec amendment bill. Some of those who took part were Burke, Charles James Fox and Sheridan. It was in that debate, when Canadian constitutional development was discussed for the first time, that the great schism took place between Burke and Fox. Friends they had been; enemies they became that day, and they never spoke again.
It was in that debate that Burke gave his definition of a party. I am not quoting him at the moment, but in essence a party is constituted when members decide for reasons that seem good to them to band together in support of or in opposition to certain principles.
Someone has said that names mean little, and reference was made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) to 1940. If you look at the red book of that year you will find the Conservative party was elected under the name of the national party, the national government party. The hon. member has told the house something of the changes that took place. Changes also took place within his own party. In 1940, when I came in here as a member, that party's leader was Mr. Woodsworth. Then he ceased to be the leader and another leader took his place in the person of Mr. Coldwell. It is not a question of who is leader.
The determination as to whether there is a party is one that is dependant on a number of members uniting in support of a group of principles. That being so, then the method by which the party is formed is of no consequence to parliament. If they want to fight among themselves as to whether the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) or the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette)-sitting together there in amity- should be leader, then that is a matter for themselves.
Parliament simply determines one question as to how these parties shall be seated, and this house is confronted with a situation where one group is a self-declared party

supporting certain principles and opposing certain others. The other group is smaller now, but still contends it represents the party that embraced all of them a few short months ago.
It is very interesting to think of the ecclesiastical divisions that have taken place throughout the ages. Hon. members may recall the famous case in Scotland, the Wee Free's, in the latter part of the nineteenth century, where a small group broke away from the greater church and contended that they themselves represented the tenets, traditions and abiding principles of their church. I think the courts held that a group can break away and themselves be actual, true exponents of the true religion. Which of these two groups has the true political religion I do not know. It is not for parliament to determine what is orthodoxy and what is heresy in Social Credit.
The assertion that a party cannot be formed unless it has gone through the firing line of an election campaign is certainly not borne out by the experience of history. Members have been elected in one party and have gone over to another, and it would be none of our concern in parliament if the hon. member for Red Deer and those associated with him crossed the floor. Those changes are not the questions to be determined by parliament.
The assertion that a party cannot be recognized unless it has fought an election and fielded a certain number of candidates would create a condition of affairs wherein members would be bound into forced allegiance until such time as they were able to go before the electorate, and to accept the recommendations of the committee in this regard would be a travesty on parliament.
How can this house say to the fewer, "Your position shall be a senior one in the house"? That is what they are asking, and it would make a mockery of parliament. We would be placing parliament in the position of saying to any group, however small, "If you can command the support of the majority of the House of Commons your position shall be senior to any other party." If we accept this principle then the official opposition, with 96 members, might very well be removed from its present position. In actuality it would not be, but if this theory were accepted, and if the government had a large majority, it could determine that the opposition should sit in the far end of the chamber, whatever its numbers.
To accept the report in its present form would be, as I said a moment ago, a travesty on parliament. A political party is self-created, self-constituted, until such time as its members are removed by the electorate from the political scene.
Privileges and Elections
I do not think we would have had this difficulty if it had not been for the amendment to the House of Commons act that was passed a few months ago. Section 42 of that act now says:
There shall be paid to each member of the House of Commons, other than the Prime Minister or the member occupying the recognized position of Leader of the Opposition in the House of Commons, who is the leader of a party that has a recognized membership of twelve or more persons in the House of Commons, an allowance at the rate of $4,000 per annum in addition to the sessional allowance payable to such member.
It must be disheartening to some to lose the position that qualified them for this, not by the effluxion of time or action of the electorate but rather by action of the members themselves.
Therefore in so far as the fourth part of the recommendation is concerned, that the question of the privileges to be enjoyed by a group be referred to the parliamentary counsel of the House of Commons for study and report to the Speaker, it flies in the face of our jurisprudence. Is parliament to say what the law is? Is a parliamentary counsel to say? This is a matter for interpretation.
It can be submitted simply to the courts, and it should be submitted to the courts. On the one hand you have the hon. member for Red Deer, now with 11 members, and the hon. member for Villeneuve with more than 12 members. This question should not be submitted to parliamentary counsel to interpret the law. To me it is very clear. I am not giving any interpretation of the law, but I say that if the $4,000 was not dangling before their eyes-

I would ask those who write that way to read the debates of 1910 and 1911: parliament sitting night and day for weeks on end; Sir Wilfrid Laurier, annoyed, angered and aroused as a result of what he thought was unfair; Sir Robert Borden followed a different course. You know, Mr. Speaker, the best debates we ever had were on Friday nights. I think the motion made today may lead to very good debates. It was on Friday nights, when we were unencumbered by some members who found it necessary to be elsewhere, that parliament was really at its best. We used to have some great debates. I look back to those days and in a reminiscent mood, with nostalgic memories of the past, I say that those were great days in the House of Commons. They are no different today. The level of debate is just as high, or higher, today as it was then, although each generation looks back at the previous one and says 
how much better it used to be. Parliament spent, not hours but days and days, night and day, debating amendment after amendment. In those days, too, the press reported to a degree that does not exist today. About a week ago I was sent a number of newspapers of 1911 and 1912. They contain pages of reports on parliament. What everybody said was mentioned in some particular. Things have changed. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam said today, "Well, have they changed for the better?"
I want to say this to those who criticize parliament, that the members today discharge their responsibilities as effectively and as efficiently as they ever did. This does not mean that changes in the rules must not be made. We have tried over and over again to bring about changes. When you are sitting over there in the government benches you say, "I wonder what those chaps in the opposition are up to" when they ask for these things; and when they endeavour to bring something forward, we know with certainty there must be some reason. All of us want to make parliament more effective; but we will not make parliament more effective by going about this country and speaking in disparaging tones about it. Mind you, Mr. Speaker, when the indemnity was raised to $18,000 it was said this would bring better members into parliament. I wonder which hon. member is prepared to admit that anybody could take his place.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was indeed pleased to hear the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), in speaking to this motion, refer to the great customs and traditions of the mother of parliaments at Westminster. At the same time I was somewhat surprised when he then said that it was a heresy to propose a seating arrangement such as that set out in the committee's report. I would, with all respect, invite the right hon. gentleman's attention to the seating arrangements in the British house of commons in November of 1922. After the election on that occasion the labour party was returned with 138 members and the liberal party, under the Right Hon. Herbert Henry Asquith, could only show up with 60 members. That parliament, the great mother of parliaments with all its customs and traditions, accepted a seating arrangement whereby the liberal party under Mr. Asquith with only 60 seats was given the front bench of the 28902-5-234
Privileges and Elections official opposition and Ramsay Macdonald's 138 members accepted a secondary position.
Therefore, with great respect, sir, I say that the seating arrangement proposed in this report can be justified and sanctioned not only by practice in the halls of Westminster but also in this house. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) alluded to the Liberal party, and may I say to him that hon. members on this side of the house will vote on this matter as freely, as fairly and as dispassionately as any group in this house.
I would invite the attention of this house to the fact that Mr. Speaker posed the question to this house, which is to be found at page 3007 of Hansard:
Have we a new party according to this new definition...? To my mind this is a question for the house to decide.
A reading of the report makes it abundantly clear that the committee felt there was not a new party, but that there was a new group in the house; and that can be justified on the evidence. This difficult problem was made somewhat less difficult because the Speaker, as mentioned by the Leader of the Opposition, had provided us with a definition of the word "party" as follows:
"Party"... is a body of men united for promoting the national interest on some particular principle in which they are all agreed.
It is my humble opinion that it was not the duty of the committee to disentangle and to isolate all the internal differences between the two factions warring within the bosom of the Social Credit party. We have to determine on broad general principles the differences in the political complexions of these two groups.
May I direct your attention, Mr. Speaker, first of all to a letter sent by the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette), which is as follows:
Following the annual convention of the Rallie-ment des creditistes in Granby, Quebec, on August 31 and September 1, 1963, it is my duty to inform you that our political group will hereafter sit as a separate group in the House of Commons.
And that is precisely the finding of the committee, that it was a separate group and not a new political party.
But may I say that there is more cogent and compelling evidence than even that. May I again draw the attention of the house to the evidence given by the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire). This is what he said in reply to a question by the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue, as set out in the committee report of the evidence:
