speechtext:
The national Social Credit party
is our party, so the answer is yes.
We are therefore confronted with this dilemma. We have one group claiming that they

Privileges and Elections are the Social Credit party, and we have another group claiming that they are the Social Credit party. It is not a matter of difference in political conviction, because the group under the leadership of the hon. member for Villeneuve still say that they are pledged to the same political conviction as when they were elected. It is really a matter of difference in leadership. So the situation arises that there are two groups both pledging themselves to the same political conviction, the one under the leadership of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson), and the "Johnnie-come-latelies", if I may use that expression, under the leadership of the hon. member for Villeneuve. I submit that on the strength of this evidence the committee was left with no alternative but to say that there was another group in this house.
May I again go back to the mother of parliaments of November, 1922. In the election held at that time there were two groups of the liberal party, that under the Right Hon. H. H. Asquith and that under the leadership of Mr. David Lloyd George. That parliament held that there was a national liberal party and a liberal group under the leadership of David Lloyd George, and so I would reaffirm and reiterate that the findings of this committee have been sanctioned and justified by tradition and custom both here and elsewhere.
Having answered that question, Mr. Speaker, the committee next turned its attention to the question of the seating arrangements. Let me say to this house, Mr. Speaker, that no one in that committee closed his mind to the question of numerical strength. I would point out that in 1935 there were 17 members in this house representing the Social Credit party, and 14 sitting as C.C.F. members, the predecessors of the New Democratic party. It is my understanding, although I am subject to correction on this, that the house then accepted a seating arrangement whereby the 14 C.C.F. members were given priority over the 17 Social Credit members, and that arrangement was acquiesced in by the right hon. gentleman who now leads the official opposition.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not want to interrupt-I have been following the hon. gentleman very carefully and with interest-but I was not in the house at that time.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
As one who has great respect for the Leader of Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), I apologize.
The seating arrangements at that time were justified on the broad, general ground of seniority: First, that the C.C.F. party had come into this house earlier than the Social Credit party; next, that its membership was drawn from a larger number of provinces

and, finally, that the services of the individual members had extended over a great number of years. It is my humble contention that those same arguments can be applied with equal force to the seating arrangements in this chamber today. To assume for one moment that the majority in the committee recommended moving the New Democratic party next to the official opposition solely on the grounds of the numerical strength of that party would not be accurate. We justified this recommendation on other grounds. I ask hon. members to note that the disparity in numbers is extremely small-17 as against 13, and 11. It may be that had the difference in numbers been greater we would not have given weight to other considerations, but on this occasion we justified placing the New Democratic party next to the official opposition because they were senior to the other minority groups, because its representatives here were drawn from three provinces and because the services of its individual members have extended over many years.
Let me point out that of the members led by the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette), apart from the hon. member himself, none can claim to have served in more than two parliaments. At least three or four can claim that distinction in the party led by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson). In addition, the hon. member for Red Deer can claim members from the provinces of British Columbia, Alberta and Quebec. On the other hand, the members united under the leadership of the hon. member for Villeneuve-and I do not say this in a disparaging manner-are limited to representing the province of Quebec. Let me further point out that the group united under the leadership of the hon. member for Red Deer came into this house under his leadership. They accepted it and the situation was acquiesced in by all members.
I repeat, the difference in the number of members is small, only 13 as against 11. Moreover, we have no assurance that this disparity will remain the same. Thus I say that although this report may not be without its imperfections, and few reports are, whatever those imperfections may be this recommendation can be justified on grounds of logic, common sense, tradition and custom.
Finally, may I turn to the question of the privileges enjoyed by the group under the leadership of the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette). If any hon. member thinks that this report, or its acceptance, constitutes an attempt to prejudice the rights of any minority group in this house, let him disabuse himself of that idea at once. It is my understanding, as a new and humble

member, that the rights and privileges enjoyed here, whether by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), by the Leader of the Opposition or by an ordinary backbencher all flow from the Speaker's chair following the course of custom and tradition. It is my respectful submission that the same rights and privileges should flow to all minority groups in this house and that they should not be catalogued or made the subject of an inventory by any of the groups represented here. After all, why should their rights and privileges be different from those extended to any members of the house down through the years?
Before concluding what I have to say I should like to deal with the other point which was raised by the Leader of the Opposition when he referred to the indemnity of $4,000 payable under the House of Commons Act and Senate Act. In my respectful opinion this does not raise a question as to the privileges enjoyed by members of this house. This is why the committee was prompted in its decision to refer this particular matter to parliamentary counsel, in order that advice might be given to the Speaker; we considered this was not a matter to be dealt with by the committee.
I had, personally, hoped that this question might be dealt with without regard to party distinction, but despite the fact that I am a new member I have already learned that to expect such a thing to happen would be a triumph of hope over experience.

Mr. Speaker, the question we are discussing this afternoon would have really required only a few minutes of attention and thinking, perhaps, to arrive at a decision.
I submit that if the members of the house, on the government side as well as on the opposition side, know their arithmetic well enough to tell whether 12 or 13 is more than 11, none could say really that we have to ask any political party permission to be recognized as members of parliament elected by our constituents.
I highly appreciate the remarks that were made a little while ago, by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), as well as the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker).
As for the hon. member for Brant-Haldi-mand (Mr. Pennell), who tried to make us understand there had been recognized seniority in the house around 1945, I know that among the group of 23 Social Credit members who sit presently in the house, I was the only member sitting from 1946 to 1949. If there is seniority somewhere, I am of the opinion 28902-5-234J
Privileges and Elections that we have it in our movement. But that is not the point.
The committee on privileges and elections mentions a special question to be considered, and it is this: Are we going to recognize a new party which developed during this parliament, since the election?
That is the only point on which we have to make a decision and report to the Speaker in order that the dispute be settled. There is the point, the whole question referred to the committee on privileges and elections.
As for the committee, its report is completely off the beam. It says that members of the New Democratic party should come after those of the Conservative party, that members of the Thompson group should come after members of the New Democratic party, and lastly the Ralliement des creditistes group.
It makes no mention of the question: "Are we going to recognize a new party which developed during this parliament and since the election?"
The members of this house are aware that the Ralliement des creditistes was born in 1958, on June 4, and that, ever since, I have taken the responsibility of leader of the movement in the province of Quebec.
A while ago we heard the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Chapdelaine) say that the movement was elected under false pretences. I say to him, the hon. member for Sherbrooke, and to all those who think the same way today, that if it were not for the Ralliement des creditistes, none of them would sit in this house now.
As the hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Lessard)-whose absence I regret-mentioned, and the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Cote) would agree, they were chosen as candidates of the Ralliement des creditistes. Here is his letter dated September 12, 1963, when he wrote:
"I accepted to be candidate for the Ralliement des creditistes in Lake St. John-*"
He did write: "Ralliement des creditistes", and not the Social Credit association.
The movement affiliated to the Social Credit Association of Canada, that is the Social Credit, never existed, no more than there is a Social Credit party in Canada. What existed in Quebec before the reorganization of the association was not the Social Credit party, keep that in mind, but the Ralliement des creditistes of the province of Quebec. The Ralliement existed before. It all started with the Ralliement des creditistes in the province of Quebec; and without the contribution of the Ralliement des creditistes my hon. English speaking friends from Alberta would probably not be here today.
Mr. Speaker, why not ask those people from Alberta or Quebec who are followers of

Privileges and Elections the hon. member for Red Deer whether they hold membership cards issued by the national association? Such a thing does not even exist. Why not ask them? They say that we have been elected under false pretences. Ask them what kind of membership card they have in their pocket. Those cards identify them as active members of the Ralliement des credi-tistes du Quebec. They don't have any card from the national association.
Mr. Speaker, on page 21 of the report of the committee on privileges and elections I see that the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Girouard) introduced a suggestion or a motion. Here is what he said:
And at this time I wish to point out that I am only acting on the invitation of the Speaker. My motion is as follows:
That a group of members which did not form a party at the time of the last general election cannot be recognized as a party before facing the electorate as such.
The member for Labelle should tell us, whether when he became a candidate in the riding of Labelle, he asked permission from the hon. member for Red Deer or from the hon. member for Villeneuve. Further, what organization in his riding had him elected? Was it the Ralliement des creditistes of Labelle county or the national organization of the Canadian Social Credit party?
If you want other evidence, Mr. Speaker, I can supply you with loads of it to establish the existence of the true Social Credit in this Parliament in Ottawa. It is due to the effort of the Ralliement du credit social and the Social Crediters in the province of Quebec that this party is represented in this house. I have the evidence right here.
Let us see what the popular vote was at the last election-

Gone down? Open your ears and your eyes and listen to this: The popular vote increased by 56,000 in the province of Quebec, on April 8, 1963, compared with June 18, 1962. I do not want to rub it in, but I only want to set the record straight.
In Quebec, le Ralliement des creditistes obtained a total of 571,333 votes. I challenge the member for Red Deer to come and tell us the percentage of votes he obtained for Quebec.
Let us look at the province of Nova Scotia where the national organization was operating. Three hundred and sixty seven votes were given to the Social Credit party in the whole province of Nova Scotia.
In New Brunswick, out of a total of 232,000 votes, 20,194 were for the Social Credit candidates.
In Quebec out of a total of 2,096,000 votes, over 29 per cent or 571,000 were cast in favour of the Social Credit party.

In the province of Ontario, where the national organization worked their hands raw and spent their funds to convince the Ontario voters of the value of the Social Credit doctrine, out of 2,721,984 votes, the Social Credit got only 55,758 votes.
In Manitoba, 27,796 votes out of 386,000.
In Saskatchewan, out of 405,720 electors, the total of Social Credit votes for the national association-and mind you the president of the national association lives in Saskatchewan -a vice president or a treasurer, a Mr. Daryl Rumble, took exactly the startling total of 566 votes in the riding of Assiniboia, in the southern part of Saskatchewan. Total for Saskatchewan: 14,819 votes.
In Alberta, a province where there has been a provincial Social Credit administration in power for 30 years, out of a total of 468,000 votes, the Social Crediters won 125,642 votes. The percentage is less than what we took in Quebec.
In British Columbia, out of a total of 578,000 electors, the Social Crediters took 82,000 votes, and that, with a Social Credit provincial administration in power for the last 13 years. The Progressive Conservatives, the Liberals and even the N.D.P. were ahead of the Social Credit national association.
To sum up, out of a total of seven million electors in Canada, we took 571,000 votes in Quebec against 327,000 votes for the national organization in the other provinces.
Mr. Speaker, those are facts and statistics quoted here to show to what degree they are trying today to minimize those who gave a new lease on life to a political movement.

I know very well that if I asked the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis) what he thinks of our movement, he would wish for its disappearance tomorrow morning, but I would say the same thing about the Liberals. Mr. Speaker, as an independent member, I would like to express some independent ideas on the problem now before us, but I want, more particularly, to rise above every personal consideration and every political advantage from which a group in this house might benefit.
We are told that this is an important question, but I am not ready to admit that statement, only that it is a matter of consequence, which means that the decision taken today, or tomorrow, or in six months from now, will have repercussions in any future debate which might take place in the house if it had to face an identical issue.
We know that British procedure is based on a great number of precedents. This precedent, which might or might not be created here, will have extraordinary consequences in the future.
But I would like, here, to tell the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that I have as much admiration for him as all the others, and in this all hon. members in this house will support me, even if he said that some considered him a nuisance. As far as I am concerned, I do not think so. For, even if it might sometimes be said that our business has been to a certain extent delayed by his remarks, we recognize his integrity and ability.
Yet, I think that today-and, after all, he might make a mistake even after several years of parliamentary experience-he voiced somewhat dangerous implications in the house, when he suggested that the fact of not recognizing that new group would jeopardize democratic rights, and that it was an impingement on free speech.
Such a thing has never been considered.
The matter which the committee and the house have to decide, is not so much to know whether or not there should be deprivation of the right of speech, but to see whether the new party which has, as we

know now, been formed following the last election is to be recognized or not.
As you realize, my argument is entirely above the parties or the persons concerned. This is a question of principle. And I would even say that if the division had decided that the group we still recognized as the Social Credit would include 15 members and the other group, nine members, there would be no more reason to recognize the new group than there is today. It is merely a question of parliamentary procedure, which is not written in the laws, which is written nowhere, but which has built up gradually through precedents over the years.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker) stressed out the admiration he had for Sir Wilfrid Laurier and I suppose he has the same consideration for the right hon. Mr. King. And Mr. King himself said -I shall not quote his remarks word for word not to take too much of the time of the house-that he would not contribute in the house to the establishment of new parties because this would lead to anarchy.
As for democracy, it is something that is built up at the constituency level by the voters. We are elected by democratic procedure. And in the House of Commons, we must follow the regulations even if they are coercive.
I remember last year, when I was whip of the party, and I would meet with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre; in order to decide about the number of speakers that would take part in a debate, after consultation, we would agree on three Conservatives, two Liberals, one member of the New Democratic party and one Crediter. But, afterwards, if there was a change, nobody clamoured that his rights were flouted or that he had been deprived of his democratic rights. All followed or stuck to what had been agreed upon or set up in advance.
I should like to draw to the hon. members' attention the fact that the suggestion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is very clever, most misleading- I do not mean like the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette), especially, but most misleading.
The point is not to determine the privileges of the present members, but the privileges of a recognized group. It is known that there are privileges and concessions which are granted out of courtesy and not out of respect for democracy. The legislation which set them up is nothing other than precedents.
It is said that the government must take its responsibilities. That is another way of changing the subject. Those who have to take responsibilities are the members of parliament. Legislation is passed by parliament and not

by the government. When the Conservatives had 208 members in the house, it was not the Conservative party or the government which passed the legislation, but parliament.
The hon. member tor Winnipeg North Centre suggested that parties are not mentioned anywhere in the election procedure. I imagine that this did not happen only in my own riding. But the hon. member is so well informed.
However, when I reported to the returning officer in my constituency, I had to state the name of the group for which I was running. I could have written Conservative, Liberal, N.D.P. or Social Credit. I would have to go and see the returning officer to see the form I filled out to indicate under what label I was running. I was running for the Social Credit party.
I must also say that the posters we affixed as long as we were allowed to do so, also had the name of the Social Credit party printed on them.
It does not follow that because a group with a provincial name joined a national group for the purpose of an election, should not be recognized as a national party. Nobody ever challenged this. It is for us to decide whether it is in the public interest and in the interest of the country's future to recognize any new party which has never been through a general election, not even a byelection.
In this connection, I shall recall the words of Mackenzie King who said following a by-election where one more member had been elected to parliament: "It is not because a candidate won a by-election that he should be recognized as a group." There is no reason for that. Precedents can be set and can become law as far as our procedure is concerned. If we make a decision that alters the meaning and the spirit of the previously established procedure, we shall create a precedent that others will put forward.
The Leader of the Opposition referred earlier to Mr. Manion who was elected to parliament, became party leader and was replaced by Mr. Hanson while still sitting in the house. This simply proves that the party had chosen a new leader, it does not prove that the new party leader was recognized or that this new member of parliament or this new leader had formed a new party.
Now, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre proceeded with his logical demonstration and he finally put the blame on the Liberals, whether the Liberals were to accept the committee's recommendations or not, while in the remainder of his speech he tried to prove that we were not members of a party, but rather individuals elected as such.
Privileges and Elections I do not see why the responsibility should be taken from a party to be shifted upon a member, and then taken from a member to be thrown again upon a party.
I think the hon. member forgot what he had said previously in his speech when he came to that pathetic appeal, when he pleaded the cause of the Ralliement des creditistes.
Then, Mr. Speaker, I do not want to speak at too great length on the subject. As a French Canadian from the province of Quebec, I merely wanted to prove that regardless of parties, regardless of the motion, it is possible to calmly debate a subject of such importance which will be of such consequence.
I wish to associate myself with the words of the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Girouard) and say that I believe that I am a first class Canadian, a first class French Canadian. I also believe that I am a first class representative of the province of Quebec and I intend to work for the province of Quebec as much as for the remainder of the country, because I consider that I am part of a whole and that I am also part of another whole as far as the province of Quebec is concerned.
I wish everyone to know and especially that it appear in Hansard that it is not because we are logical with ourselves that we should be considered as traitors, or as abdicators or as renegades or as those who give up their own nationality to gather around racists. No.
The arguments which I put forth, because I am alone, and I think it is the first time that I have the honour of speaking on behalf of my party, are merely intended to bring back the debate on a logical basis.
And what will happen in the province of Quebec where newspapermen still wish to grant recognition to the Ralliement des creditistes not in a spirit of justice, but to be in a better position to demolish them? Even if these people try to put forward some arguments in favour of the recognition of a fourth party, in my opinion, we should not care, because there will certainly be some consequences, in one way or another, in all constituencies and even outside Quebec.
Consequently, let us assume our responsibilities and let us limit ourselves to the consideration of the present problem and not of another completely different one. We should not be afraid. The members of the government side and those of the official opposition should make their own decisions and vote freely. In my opinion, nothing can stand in the way of such a position, if we really want to settle this problem in a democratic way.
Mr. Speaker, before closing, I wish to deal with another matter.
This afternoon, reference was made to the years 1891, 1910 and 1911. May I recall to the house that at that time there were no

Some of our friends opposite seemed to attach a lot of importance to tradition and brought out the historical argument that we should not forget that the step the house was about to take was of the utmost importance for the future.
Mr. Speaker, in the early part of the present session, time and time again, we offered suggestions for the revision of our parliamentary procedure, and I think we all agree that such a revision is necessary.
I also believe that perhaps we should stop considering only tradition when the time has come to defend a cause. It seems to me we should turn our eyes toward the future. And I say to my hon. friends opposite as well as to those on this side of the house that the political future of our country should be regarded not as something to be taken for granted but as something to be looked after now.
The fact is that, in accord with democratic procedure, the Canadian people send representatives to this house at the national election. At that time, only the names of the candidates appear on the ballots; no mention is made of party allegiance.
And if we cast a glance at the future of our country, I feel we must cease giving so much importance to this tradition or to this

two-party system. The existence of a political group such as the New Democratic party or the Creditistes should be recognized as an actual fact.
After all, whether we be Liberal, Conservative, Social Crediters or members of the New Democratic party, are we not the elected representatives of the Canadian people in this house?
By the way, it is probably with such a vision of the future that on the 28th of June last, Bill No. C-91 was introduced, tending to the recognition as a group in this house of a party of 12 members in the House of Commons under the direction of a leader recognized as such by them.
Mr. Speaker, one seems to be bound by tradition when one finds it suitable, otherwise one does not think of it any more.
The hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Marcoux) said earlier in his remarks that we should uphold tradition. But, at the end of his speech, he is not interested in it any longer.
He gave as an example simultaneous interpretation and asked hon. members whether they would prefer to go back to the old days and have the interpretation system abolished. Yet, he himself had suggested a little earlier that we go back. I wonder, then, whether he was not contradicting himself.

As for the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Girouard) he did nothing but whine. I could not quite make out what he wanted to say.
Since he has good friends on this side of the house, I was wondering whether he was not turning his back on those who were his friends until lately.
The hon. member for Labelle should remember that he represents the riding that sent Henri Bourassa to the House of Commons.
Moreover, not so long ago, that constituency was represented by an independent who was a member of a fairly nationalist group.
Mr. Speaker, hon. members should not imagine that nationalism is the only thing we think about. On the contrary, we think as Canadians. And to refute an argument that was raised this afternoon to the effect that our group consists only of members from the province of Quebec, I would ask: Is the province of Quebec not part of confederation? Is the province of Quebec not part of the Canadian nation?

As members of the federal parliament, we have a right to speak for the people, to be respected and to account for our mandate to our constituents.
Mr. Speaker, by means of arguments which I would call absurd, the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Chapdelaine) has tried to illustrate the nonsense of the situation with which we are faced today. But I wonder what would be the issue if he and all the supporters of the hon. member for Red Deer who were elected with the help of the Rallie-ment des creditistes went before the electorate.
Mr. Speaker, anyone wishing to know anything about the Ralliement des creditistes only has to refer to the records of the returning officer for each riding or those of the chief electoral officer and he will see all the receipts for expenses made during the general election of June 18, 1962, and that of April 8, 1963. Official receipts, signed by an officer of the Ralliement des creditistes will be also found, accounting for all election expenses incurred in any county in the province of Quebec.
Besides, a simple check with television stations will show what programs were reserved and paid for by the Ralliement des creditistes.
Therefore, we are compelled to admit that we have been elected in our respective counties, under the name of candidates or members of the Ralliement des creditistes, even if the name of a party did not appear on each ballot.
To say that we act in bad faith and under false pretences is wrong. In fact, in my county I am known as the member of the Ralliement des creditistes, during election time as well as afterwards.
I feel it is my duty-as it is the duty of any member in this house-to be a true representative of the people, and to make their wishes heard from one end of the country to the other.
Mr. Speaker, it has even been said that we are separatists. We are simply striving to defend the rights of Canadians, of all Canadians,. and we are known as Canadians throughout the country.
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed very strange that after some speeches we have heard here, the press has followed suit, and spoken of a split in our party. A year ago everybody seemed to be waiting just for that. People were wondering who would come first, the member for Villeneuve, with his 26 followers from the province of Quebec, or the member for Red Deer and his three members from the west?
Everybody was hoping for a split. When it became obvious that we were taking a firm stand, because we could see eye to eye on certain points of organization, or on a few
Privileges and Elections basic tenets, people started to lament and seem to listen more willingly to the whining we heard a moment ago, to the effect that we are divided.
If we are divided, I feel that in view of the principles of democracy, it does not belong to political opponents or to those who are sitting on the house committee and who act as witnesses and judges to make decision.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that we are answerable to our constituents. Thus, I believe that we should forget all partisan politics and consider the political action taken as far as legality is concerned. Then, let us restrict our discussion to legality under Bill C-91 which was passed on July 26 last and which, for the first time in Canada, defines what a parliamentary group is entitled to in the House of Commons, that is a group comprising 12 persons is entitled to have a leader recognized by parliament.
If we want to base our judgment on that, I believe that we will very soon find a solution, while it will be the opposite if we start entertaining all sorts of considerations and if we consider traditions.
In addition to legality, let us also examine the issue in terms of the future. It is good to examine the past, but we must also face the future.
As I said at the beginning, if the two-party system is a thing of the past, I still believe that we should look to the future so as to find ways to establish a political continuity in this house. If the continuity in the house is to be ensured according to standards of democracy, I believe that it is time for us to recognize the rights and privileges of other parties in the house, as defined by Bill C-91.
The two-party system has prevailed here since 1867, this I will grant. Through the operation of that system, the ball was tossed back and forth and the parties were charging each other with all sorts of things, and the same charges were picked up by the official opposition when it was its turn to act in that capacity, and when it had a chance to get back into office, it was the target for the charges levelled at them by the party which had moved across the floor to make up the official opposition.
Six months ago, charges were simply displaced by a change in the seating arrangement in the house.
The two-party policy has come to an end in Canada. Let us now look at the political future of this country from another angle. The parliamentary policy of the house is not unknown to the community.
Last autumn, when the session started on September 27,	1962, all political groups
advocated a revision of the rules dealing with

Privileges and Elections parliamentary procedure. Let us therefore recognize the groups representing the voice of the people in this house: those groups are certainly entitled to a better future, that of a party or group which can vote, or if it wants to do so, impede the progress of public business in the house.
Parliamentary procedure to be approved today should be considered in this light. We are living in the twentieth century. Different ideologies are abroad in the world.
Let us admit in this house the voice of the people who have the right to be heard through their representatives, in order to attain a continuity of economic and parliamentary thinking in Canada. We should try to reach this aim and proceed with a full revision of our standing orders.
I therefore ask for a recognition based on justice and legal order, as defined in Bill C-91, which was approved by hon. members.
On that basis let us give relief to those who ask for justice, and let us stop talking about a thousand and one things except the problem which is now pointing towards the future and has to be considered carefully tonight, before taking the step which will definitely ratify the recognition of a group in this house, even if at this time that group is only represented by 13 members from the province of Quebec.
If we wish to keep the province of Quebec within the frame of confederation, Mr. Speaker, I think we should all unite more than ever and look towards the future in the hope of securing a revision of the rules and regulations of the house which would recognize the wishes of the people through the instrumentation of the various groups in the House of Commons. Whatever their position, these groups deserve and demand recognition. They base their claims upon Bill No. C-91, under the terms of which they demand justice based upon logic.

That was the question referred by the Chair to the committee and to this house to decide. It is not merely a question of seating, if I might say so with the greatest respect to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles); it is not merely a question of the physical arrangements of this house. If I might eliminate two issues at the outset from the crucial question before the house, I would say this. First of all the question of who gets the $4,000 payable to a leader of a party having at least 12 members, under the recent amendment to the Senate and House of Commons Act, is not a question that could properly be decided by either the committee or this house, and I think on that point all members of the committee were in agreement. In other words, this is a public statute; this is a statute that has to be followed by the comptroller of the treasury, and the comptroller of the treasury may of course refer the matter to the Deputy Minister of Justice. In any event, the matter of the $4,000 additional allowance is not a question before the committee or the house at this time.
As for the seating, the physical arrangements in the house, this goes merely to the

physical arrangements and it is not and should not be interrelated with the question of status or privileges to be conceded, or allowed, or granted to a new group in this house. The committee's report as submitted to the house does not decide whether the privileges of the house-that is to say, the privileges with regard to debate, orders of the day, or motions-are to be given to a new group. It merely recognizes that as a physical fact there is an independent group, independent of the existing Social Credit party, and for that reason it would be better for the good order of the house to seat them separately. It does not prejudge the case of whether the 13 members who left the Social Credit party proper are independents, or are necessarily a new group for the purpose of recognition by the house.
The main issue still before the committee and this house is, shall this new group of 13 independents, or 13 followers of the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) be recognized as eligible for the privileges of the house? Within that context let us examine just what the committee did. First of all, it decided the seating arrangement as between the three smaller groups-the New Democratic party, the Social Credit party and the Ralliement des creditistes, or followers of the hon. member for Villeneuve. The committee had a straight choice. It could have chosen to seat those three groups either in order of numerical preference, or in order of seniority or historical precedence. The committee chose to report to this house that they be seated in order of historical precedence.

As X say, this committee, and in turn the House of Commons when it receives our report, have these two types of precedents, one, that history and seniority of groups, which was followed in 1935 and in 1940, is the proper precedent, and two, numerical strength of the groups, as was followed in 1962 and 1963, is the precedent to be followed. The committee can decide either way.
Privileges and Elections In other words, there is nothing sacrosanct about either the way the committee reported to the house or, with the greatest respect, about the way the amendment is phrased.

Our party was the oldest party and the members were the oldest members-

It is quite understandable, Mr. Speaker, why the hon. member for Winnipeg North

Privileges and Elections Centre takes such a flexible position, because for him and his party it is "Heads I win, tails you lose", either on historical precedence or numerical preference, in the light of this situation. With the whole range of facts before this house neither he nor his party could lose.
In other words, there has been no breach of principle as alleged by the parties opposite. The committee was entitled in its good judgment, after reviewing all the facts, to choose either of two sets of precedents before the house, and as a matter of fact it chose the precedent having the longest validity in this House of Commons and indeed in the house at Westminster.
There is some danger in following the amendment suggested and moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. If we were to rely on numerical strength only, with the present strength of adhesion of the two groups to the dispute, namely Social Credit and Ralliement des creditistes, we do not know whether we would be playing a game of musical chairs, because we do not know how long the adhesive tape would hold.

Villeneuve, this depends on whether this house is going to recognize this new group for the purpose of according it the privileges of this house. It is not merely a question of fact. It is not a question of whether there are 13 members or whether they profess loyalty to the hon. member for Villeneuve. Neither is it a question whether it is a new group. The question is: Is this group such that this house should at this moment give recognition to it for the purposes of the procedure of this House of Commons? It is not, as I say, just a question of fact; it is a question of recognition by this house.

Mr. Speaker, in all fairness I think I have been generous already in diluting my time for the benefit of questioners. If there is any time left later on I will be glad to submit to the interrogation of the hon. member for Lapointe.
Now, Mr. Speaker, looking at this question of recognition for the purposes of the procedure of this house, this has serious implications. This is why the question was worthy of being submitted to parliamentary counsel for the advice and guidance of Your Honour. Why do I say it has serious implications? First of all, there is the danger that recognition of these 13 members as a new group would contribute to the eventual fragmentation of this house. Many commentators in newspapers have said: Give them their way; recognize them, and get on with the business of the house. But the committee feared that to do so would be to open the door to the kind of splintering of parliament which destroyed the parliament of France under the third and fourth republics.

If the committee and the house were to give recognition to a group which has not received recognition by the electorate as being a group we would, I believe, be creating a precedent which would have dire results. There is nothing in the traditions, precedents or conventions of this house which demands that you, Mr. Speaker, should recognize the formation of new political parties or groups, or that you should accept breakaways from political parties already in existence during the life of a

current parliament. Only the people can create a party; and until the people have recognized, in an election, the existence of this new grouping I think it is within the rights of the committee and of the house to refuse to grant recognition.

The Leader of the Opposition had something to say about this question this afternoon. He said, first of all, that the committee refused to face the issue. Let me say, in answer to that, that the committee did reach a decision, despite the fact that the party which the right hon. gentleman leads wanted to avoid the issue. I could quote from page 82 of the transcript of evidence before the committee. The hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) had this to say:
All I can see is internal strife within a political party and as such it is something which this committee should not meddle with and indeed, I doubt whether it has the power to do so.
In other words, the position taken by the Conservative party was that the matter should be sent back to the Speaker, with no action being taken whatsoever. The Leader of the Opposition quoted the famous maxim of Voltaire when he said: I do not agree with a word that you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it. The answer to this, with the greatest respect, is that there is here no infringement of the right to speak of any member of parliament. The right of individual members to speak is untrammelled and unfettered. It is as great as it has always been. In any case it would take more than the rules of the House of Commons to silence either the hon. member for Villeneuve or the hon. member for Lapointe. The only restriction which is involved in the committee's decision is that the right to recognize certain hon. members as a group is, for the moment,

Privileges and Elections limited. The learned Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) referred to the precedent of a member of a major party crossing the floor to another major party as a precedent for recognition of this kind. With the greatest respect, that has no validity whatsoever in regard to the present argument, because one party is already recognized, as is the other. The question here is: Is a party to have recognition; not whether we are to recognize a switch from one recognized party to another recognized party.
The question before the house is, should we give in to a new grouping just because we are threatened with filibusters, just because the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) threatens that he may pull his party out of confederation. I do not think so. Fortunately, Mr. Speaker, such is not the case. This afternoon the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre proceeded to give his hit parade list of certain members he liked. He also seemed to question whether or not he was liked by the other members. I should like to assure him that I think he is not really a bad guy. This seemed to bother him, and he seemed to feel he no longer belonged or was wanted. I would not want him to have this feeling because, after all, it is a dangerous thing when people begin to wonder whether they are really wanted. None of us would want anything to happen to our good friend from Winnipeg North Centre.
The hon. member said he was making his stand on principle. I do not know that he had to say this. However, when he did say it, two questions crossed my mind. First, was this something new and, second, did he imply that those who did not agree with him were not motivated by principle? Well, Mr. Speaker, I believe that the doing of things on the basis of principle or in the right way is not the sole prerogative of any one group or any one individual. I feel strongly, on the basis of principle, that the decision taken by this committee was the right one. As I tried to understand the feeling of the people on this subject, judging from the mail I received it seemed to me that there was a body of opinion that seemed to say: Recognize this group; give them what they want for the sake of peace. This seems to me to be a very

Privileges and Elections poor reason for doing something in a particular fashion.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, in his questioning of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, was begging the question. Had the decision been to seat the group under the leadership of the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) ahead of the group under the leadership of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson), then the argument could have been made just as easily from the same quarter of this house that that was the wrong decision. As was pointed out, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre himself said in the committee that there were two courses of action. As I was looking for some leadership on this problem, I was listening to him closely. He seemed to indicate that we could decide either way. If there was a good basis for making the decision either way, what then is an individual member of the committee or of parliament to do? How are you going to vote if there are two courses of action, both of which are based on precedents? How do you arrive at the right decision? We have to decide which is the better precedent. Perhaps other hon. members in the house will disagree with my view, but surely the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will not deny me the right to express it, and I say that I fear what has happened in this regrettable situation may have some disastrous effect on future parliaments. It seems to me that the decision made now should be made with some thought as to its effect on subsequent parliaments.
Accordingly, there seems to me to be a difference. I can see a genuine distinction which perhaps others cannot see. I see a distinction in respect of a group that has candidates in every part of this country who are elected to the house under a common banner, under a common leadership, who come into this house and sit as a group elected by voters who knew they would sit as a group, and who knew they would have this man as leader. I think there is a difference between this situation and this new phenomena in which parties or groups within the House of Commons break into small groups. I think there is a distinction here. I think the precedent of recognizing the senior parties was a wise one. Accordingly, I should like to see the house adopt this report.

I know I do. This is the whole point of the amendment which the Leader of the Opposition has made to the amendment made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. We feel this clause

Privileges and Elections should be deleted because we do not think the committee had the right to refer this question to parliamentary counsel. It is not his responsibility. It is only fair to say, I think, that the first mention I heard of this matter in committee came from the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, not from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. He said this was a question to be determined by the treasury on the advice of the Department of Justice. I believe we will experience some difficulty in interpreting this particular section of Bill C-91 in which the words appear "which has a recognized membership of 12 or more persons". What does "recognized" mean? Does it mean recognition by this house? Does it mean recognition by the electorate? Does it mean recognition by those who support the group leader? Does it mean recognition individually or does it mean recognition collectively? It seems to me these words are fraught with difficulty, and this constitutes another example of the inept drafting which seems to characterize the legislation which this government is producing. I feel the amendment proposed by my right hon. friend would deal with that situation, because if the question of privileges, including the $4,000, were left to interpretation by the proper authorities, then undoubtedly those who were charged with these matters would recognize their responsibilities and discharge them. I do not think that as a committee or as the House of Commons we should be interpreting the legislation we pass.
Having made these observations, I feel the debate should now be brought to a close as quickly as possible in order that we might get on with the business we were sent here to do, as the leader of the New Democratic party has so often, in his holier-than-thou attitude, advised us to do. It seems to me the members of that particular group took a great deal of the time of the house in speaking on this subject, and without intending any offence to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas), may I say it occurs to me that his vision is often obscured by his halo slipping over his eyes.

speechtext:
The question before the house at this moment is an amendment to an amendment which calls for the complete deletion of clause 4 of the report from the standing committee on privileges and elections. Clause 4 recommends

that the question of the privileges to be enjoyed by the group under the leadership of the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) be referred to parliamentary counsel of the House of Commons for study and report to the Speaker. If I understand the terms of reference correctly, when this house referred the whole matter to the committee it was precisely because Your Honour needed some guidance in dealing with the demand for privileges which was made by the hon. member for Villeneuve following a convention in Granby. Therefore, if this section is deleted from the recommendations which have been submitted by the committee, the terms of reference will not have been complied with. In other words, the question of privileges is not answered at all in any of the other three recommendations which are made. They deal with some physical changes in the house, it is true-the seating of the various parties-but they say nothing about the privileges which have been demanded.
This debate has ranged fairly wide so far. Attempts have been made to bring up precedents for the guidance, first of the committee, and now of the house. I believe that if we have listened carefully to all the precedents which have been cited we can only reach one conclusion, namely that there is no precedent for the situation we are now facing. It is therefore up to the house to create a precedent and reach a decision to deal with a wholly novel situation. There have been attempts to draw parallels between the present situation and something else which happened, but I do not think there is any direct relationship between the problem we are now facing and anything which has happened in the past.
Some of the arrangements that have been made in the house with respect to seating and also recognition have been referred to by hon. members, particularly the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), and in every case the arrangements both for seating and for recognition have been based first of all on policies, patterns and labels that were presented to the electorate in the immediately preceding election. Surely, Mr. Speaker, we as members of the House of Commons have a responsibility to organize ourselves and conduct the business of the house in line with something that has been presented to the electors, whether it has been put down in writing or not. As far as I am concerned that is paramount in the situation. Several members have mentioned that even in the committee situations were referred to and the same persons who recited them said it was possible to draw more than one conclusion from them.

I do not intend to go over a lot of the ground that other hon. members have covered. I do think, though, that if members of the house are going to be faced with a vote to decide whether or not there is another party in the house and whether all the privileges and rights which are extended to a party are to be granted, we should be cognizant of some of the facts. The hon. member for Villeneuve delved rather deeply into this matter. He is welcome to his opinion, but I should like to place on the record another opinion with regard to some of the things that took place even before the last two elections, so that members will be completely familiar with the organization of the national Social Credit party. The constitution of the Social Credit party provides as follows with regard to membership:
Every provincial Social Credit organization or league that applies for affiliation and is accepted by the association shall, upon payment of the prescribed fees, be granted membership in the association, providing there will be only one recognized in any province.
It is quite true that the Ralliement des creditistes was a provincial organization and was accepted into the national organization, and it was the only one from the province of Quebec. In article 3 the constitution provides:
A national convention shall be held every four years, or more often as the national council shall decide.
I should like to draw to the attention of the house that the national council of the Social Credit party of Canada had a meeting in Ottawa in July of this year. I should also like to draw the attention of hon. members to the fact that all of the members of the Ralliement des creditistes who were present at the 1961 convention subscribed to these articles of the constitution.
The national council held a meeting in July, and I happen to know that representations were made to the national council by certain members of the Ralliement des creditistes demanding a national convention immediately. The national council in their wisdom decided for many reasons that they would not call a national convention at once. The fact is, of course, that the council is made up of all the Social Credit organizations across Canada and like all democratic institutions a majority vote rules the decisions made by that council.
I should also like to refer to various clauses in the constitution dealing with how a national convention shall be set up. The first provision is that there shall be five representatives from each affiliated Social Credit organization or league. This would give each province having a Social Credit organization
Privileges and Elections five voting delegates at a convention, and this is what the Ralliement des creditistes would have if they attended. Second, there shall be five representatives in good standing from each federal constituency in Canada. I should like to point out that there was an opportunity for each one of the 75 constituencies in Quebec to have five delegates from the Ralliement des creditistes at the convention. They had the opportunity to be there in 1961.

All of this was done in accordance with democratic procedures, and I believe that a similar though not identical arrangement is used by all of the national political parties. I do not know whether there is a national Liberal party or whether it is a federation of provincial parties, although I have been told it is a federation of 10 provincial Liberal parties. Privileges and Elections
Members of the New Democratic party are making noises on my left but I believe they are also organized on the same basis. 1 know, for example, that the party that is supposed to belong to them in Saskatchewan does not even have the same name. They call themselves C.C.F.-N.D.P. I was out there over the week end and I heard that for purposes of the next provincial election they are going to drop the N.D.P. part of their name. So, Mr. Speaker, whether or not the name of the Social Credit organization in Quebec was the Social Credit league of Quebec, like the Social Credit league of Ontario or Manitoba or New Brunswick, this practice is not confined to the Social Credit party. Other parties have different names.
Another point was mentioned during the debate. In Hansard on Wednesdays the names of the members are given, and their party affiliation. Somebody has mentioned that there is a member in the cabinet who I believe calls himself Liberal-Labour. So they too have different names. But the point is that if he is Liberal-Labour I think he presented himself to the electorate as such. There is no argument about the fact that the Ralliement des creditistes had full opportunity to participate in the national convention. They subscribed to the constitution. They took part in the balloting for the leader.
It is rather interesting to note that the hon. member for Villeneuve, who now claims to be leader of the Social Credit party, also ran for the national leadership of the Social Credit party. This balloting was conducted after the constitution had been accepted. It is rather interesting to note also that there were three candidates for the position of national leader of the Social Credit party. The constitution requires that before any one candidate can be named leader, he must receive 50 per cent plus 1 of the ballots. When the ballots were counted, there was sufficient support for the hon. member for Red Deer to elect him on the first ballot.

An hon. member has said they never saw the ballots. I want him to know that the hon. member for Villeneuve appointed scrutineers who watched the counting of the ballots and who concurred in the returns.
We come to the point of discussing what is a national party, who should be recognized, who should be granted privileges, and so on. I should like the members of this house to know that there was absolutely no situation here that was not subscribed to by the Ralliement. Since then they have had a convention. They have decided to dissociate themselves from the national party. Now that
[Mr. Olson.J
they have dissociated themselves from the national party, when they subscribed to its rules, policy and so on, the question is raised now, do they become a national party? It might be of interest also to members when they come to vote on this matter to know that there are seven members of the Ralliement des Creditistes who do not subscribe to this separation. The hon. member for Villeneuve referred to some statistics in connection with the last election. I am not sure what his purpose was. Perhaps it has something to do with the total popular vote.
I should like to say, in connection with these statistics, that he was apparently trying to take unto himself all of the popular vote that was accorded to all of the men who ran as Social Credit candidates in Quebec.
I should like to say that he will have to separate the votes for at least seven of those constituencies from his calculation. There have been points raised from time to time during the debate that the adoption of the committee's report will be a violation of the freedom of the members of this house. I completely disagree with that. The question before us, and what is being demanded now by the hon. member for Villeneuve, is not that the rights and privileges of members be maintained, but that he be given some rights and privileges in addition to those normally accorded to members of this house. Certainly, no one is trying to take away any of the rights or privileges of an ordinary member of this house.
In so far as clause 4 of the report is concerned, it does not completely satisfy the terms of reference handed to the committee. It seems to me that we should very soon in this parliament attempt to define a party or define a group that will be recognized in the house. The late prime minister Mackenzie King back in 1944 said that there was only the government and the opposition, and that any further recognition by the government and the Speaker is a matter of courtesy. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that this courtesy should be granted on the basis of what was presented to the electors, and there should be nothing beyond that.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to the question raised by some members as to whether or not the Ralliement des creditistes is a national party or a provincial party. I did not hear the hon. members say whether or not this federal house should recognize a provincial party or whether recognition should be confined to national parties. Certainly, up to the time of the convention in Granby in August all the evidence points conclusively to the fact that the Ralliement des creditistes was definitely a provincial party. They were affiliated with the

national Social Credit party as the Quebec wing of the national Social Credit party.

In the case of one political party, we are going to decide by the number and in the case of the others, by seniority. Then, the Liberal party is going to decide which is the older, the group led by the member for Red Deer or that of the member for Villeneuve.
Which is the older? From 1958 to 1962, there was not one Social Credit member in the house. We were all elected in 1962. Therefore, seniority goes back to 1962 and the number should decide, if not the member for Villeneuve is the oldest of the 23 Social Crediters, since he was elected in 1946; therefore, he has seniority.
Mr. Speaker, on top of all that, they are trying to make us believe that we would not have been elected under the ticket of the Ralliement des creditistes. Indeed, we have been elected as members of that group. I gave evidence to that effect before the privileges and elections committee. The point is that the old political parties have always been elected because of their campaign funds. Who contributed? Mr. So-and-so, in trust. That is how they got elected.
As for us, how did our bills get paid, Mr. Speaker? Since the treasurer of our riding is in the gallery at present, I have no hesitation to say that they were paid by treasurer so-and-so or chairman so-and-so on behalf of the Ralliement des creditistes. That fact can be checked out. The national party organization never paid a single penny in our ridings or in our province. Never. We are the ones who paid for our election.
When I hear Social Crediters who were elected with the assistance of the Ralliement des creditistes claim that they are the ones who helped us, it is my duty to deny it. Mr. Speaker, I am sure they will think otherwise at the next election when it will no longer be possible for them to vote along the lines indicated by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the Leader of the Opposition.

Mr. Speaker, I hope that the member for Lotbiniere takes his own words into consideration, when he speaks of the decorum which should prevail here.
I think that if there were not so many interruptions from the members opposite, there would be more decorum in the house.
Mr. Speaker, in concluding, I will only add one thing. We are a group of 13 members from the province of Quebec. We are not imploring without cause. We believe that we are entitled to recognition.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that in the past-the Minister of Finance who is here knows it-1 have shown fair play when necessary. I played above-board with the Liberal party as well as the other parties. I always tried to be frank with all the other members of this house and played fair when necessary.
On a particular occasion, the Minister of Finance remembers, I rose on a question of privilege. At least, at that time, I deemed advisable to use fair play with him, which I did.
I think that the Liberal members have now to decide on something more serious and important than what the committee has presented. They have to decide on a problem much more serious than that. They must decide on a principle, that is whether it is true that other members can decide for another party. I submit that point to the conscience of all hon. members of the house.
And the responsibility will fall on the shoulders of the one who will rise first on the side of the Liberal party to vote-the Prime Minister of Canada who holds a rather high position. It is he who will vote first. With him rests the responsibility to support what is being done today, namely deny its rights and privileges to a group. The responsibility will be theirs. The way they all vote will be recorded in
Privileges and Elections Hansard. The people will be able to judge them. Let them think carefully, in order to realize whether what they are plotting today is really honest. Let them wonder whether what they are plotting today is just.
Mr. Speaker, it has been suggested a while ago that we are trying to monopolize the defence of the rights of French Canadians. No, such is not the case. If the hon. member for Dollard (Mr. Rouleau) were here tonight, and the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis) knows it, he could say that we do not endeavour to monopolize that right. We even had a meeting last year with them-and they know how it had been prepared-a meeting which was attended by all hon. members from the province of Quebec, to try and claim some rights of the French Canadians.
We did not try to monopolize this right at that time. No, we wanted to share with all our colleagues of the House of Commons the right to uphold the rights of French Canadians in the house and, in Ottawa, when the opportunity presented itself. The member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville knows that very well.
We are not trying to make it a fight for nationalism or for separatism. We do not want to transform this problem into a fight to separate French Canadians from English Canadians. I myself did not want that.
When the time came for the reappointment of Mr. Gordon as president of the Canadian National Railways, I never tried to make political capital by stirring up one race against the other, I never tried to do that.
Only when questions are asked as to why 13 French Canadian members cannot be recognized in the house when, on the other hand, seven members of the New Democratic party were recognized here in 1958, we say to ourselves: why not us?
Ask yourselves those questions. I would not want to stir up a conflict, but better be careful. This time, we shall not be the ones to start the ball rolling, it will probably be the party which will decide not to recognize 13 French Canadian members in the House of Commons. We shall not be the ones to stir up that conflict, no, but it may be those who will vote to deny us our rights and privileges in this house.
Mr. Speaker, a striking example occurred the other day when an attempt was made to deny the hon. member for Villeneuve the right to speak as leader of a group of 13 on the nuclear arms question. This will happen again. Then, there are serious problems to face in all that.

Privileges and Elections
I ask the ministers here to think it over carefully before coming to a decision which could have rather serious consequences for democracy and for the rights of parliament. I know that the French Canadians are touchy where the rights of parliament are concerned and they cannot accept that the rights and privileges of a whole group should go unrecognized in the House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to waste the time of the house on a discussion of the problem, as I feel that we have deviated rather drastically from the amendment and amendment to the amendment to the motion moved by the chairman of the committee on privileges and elections.
I must state, however, that I was under the impression we were attending a Social Credit convention or a public debate between Liberals and Social Crediters.
I am still thinking about the suggestion the leader of the house (Mr. Pickersgill) made this afternoon, in order to stretch the hours of sitting of this house. It seems to me that we should have acted more consistently, and spontaneously curtailed our verbosity, our partisanship. We should have restricted ourselves to a discussion on the merits of the amendment and of the amendment to the amendment submitted to the house.
I heard the remarks of the member for Lapointe and I regret that he did not use the word divorce once. He spoke of the separation of the Caouette group from the Thompson group. I should have liked him to use the word divorce because then the Ralliement would have relinquished all ties and responsibility with the Thompson group.
Mr. Speaker, as a lawyer, you know that even after a separation, there are still ties and responsibilities. Such is not the case after a divorce.
Mr. Speaker, I just wished to say a few words to express my regret, as a French Canadian representative of the province of Quebec, for having attended a discussion that did not deal at all with the value, the logic or the merit of the resolution or of the amendment to it, but that has particularly succeeded in discrediting the representatives of the province of Quebec with our approach of the matter in a spirit of partisanship which is far from being academic.
The decision which the house must make will decide whether the Caouette group has precedence or not over the Thompson group.
I am sorry to have to remind the house, as a representative of the province of Quebec, of the irresponsibility with which the Liberal members and certain representatives of the Social Credit party have joined in the dis-

cussion, thereby belittling in the eyes of the citizens of other provinces the sense of responsibility of the Quebec electorate.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the speeches will be over soon.

I hear the Liberals applauding and that after having said a lot of nonsense and stupidities. The remarks of certain members of the Social Credit were surely not better than those of some Liberal members.
Since the beginning, the discussions seemed to hinge on two decisions. First of all, we have to decide whether there is really division between the two groups. Then, it must be established whether parliament has the power to decide in favour of a group instead of another, I ask the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chevrier) whether he could not take a few minutes to state his opinion and settle the question.
I particularly ask the house to limit interruptions and to put the question before the house; it is the most democratic way to solve the problem.
Therefore, I ask the house to vote and I hope that the group, which perhaps may not be satisfied with the decision, will consider that parliament represents democratic authority in this country, and I hope that this minority will abide by the parliament's decision, this democratic institution that we wish to preserve for a long time.
